verdict.summary:
REGULATORY ANSWER — 14 CFR § 91.151(a), VFR fuel reserve, airplane, beyond the first point of intended landing

1. DIRECT ANSWER

| Condition | Minimum fuel beyond the first point of intended landing | Expressed as time at normal cruising speed |
|---|---|---|
| Day (VFR, airplane) | 30 minutes of flight at normal cruising speed | 30 minutes |
| Night (VFR, airplane) | 45 minutes of flight at normal cruising speed | 45 minutes |

Note the structure of the rule: the reserve is measured from the first point of intended landing, not from the destination airport and not from the last en-route checkpoint. It is flight time after that point, at normal cruising speed.

2. CONTROLLING TEXT (quoted verbatim)

14 CFR § 91.151 — Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions:

"(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Source of the quoted text (three independent retrievals, all in agreement, all fetched 2026-11-15):
- 14 CFR 2026 print edition, Title 14 vol. 2, § 91.151 (govinfo PDF, sha256 25216af9b686)
- 14 CFR 2025 XML edition, § 91.151 (govinfo, sha256 7c3230319ff7)
- eCFR current, Title 14, Chapter I, Subchapter F, Part 91 (sha256 50b3b0bc67a4)
No discrepancy exists among the three; the 30-minute day and 45-minute night figures are current.

3. SCOPE AND INTERPRETATION (each point tied to the text)

3.1 "Airplane" — paragraph (a) governs airplanes. Paragraph (b)'s 20-minute rotorcraft reserve does NOT apply to an airplane, and the 20-minute figure must not be substituted for the 30/45-minute figures above. Powered-lift, gliders, balloons, and ultralights are outside this section.

3.2 "Begin a flight" — this is a pre-departure minimum, i.e., a fuel load that must already be aboard at takeoff. It is not an average, a planning target, or a post-flight benchmark. Each subsequent departure (each new flight, including each leg of a multi-leg day) must independently satisfy the rule for the conditions at that departure.

3.3 "Beyond the first point of intended landing" — the reserve is additive. Total usable fuel required at takeoff is: trip fuel to the first point of intended landing (computed considering wind and forecast weather conditions) PLUS the 30- or 45-minute reserve PLUS taxi/run-up/apu fuel. The reserve may not be counted as part of the trip fuel, and the trip fuel may not be reduced by the reserve.

3.4 "Assuming normal cruising speed" — the reserve time is converted to a distance and a fuel quantity at the airplane's normal cruising speed and the corresponding cruise fuel flow. It is NOT computed at best-endurance, best-glide, or long-range-lean speed. Using a lower speed to shrink the reserve is non-compliant with the rule's stated assumption.

3.5 "Considering wind and forecast weather conditions" — this qualifier attaches to the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing, not to the fixed 30/45-minute reserve times. The reserve is a fixed time regardless of wind; do not stretch or shrink the 30/45 minutes for headwinds or tailwinds.

3.6 Day vs. night — "night" is defined in 14 CFR § 1.1 as the period between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight as published in the Air Almanac, converted to local time. The rule keys to the time the flight is begun. It contains no proration or en-route transition provision. Where a flight will be aloft across the day-to-night boundary, the conservative and commonly accepted practice is to carry the 45-minute reserve; carrying 45 minutes satisfies the day requirement as well, since 45 > 30.

3.7 Not a substitute for § 91.3 — § 91.151 is a minimum. The pilot in command remains responsible for the safety of the flight under § 91.3, and a legal 30-minute reserve does not authorize departing into conditions where 30 minutes is inadequate.

4. CONVERSION TO FUEL QUANTITY (procedure and worked examples)

Procedure:
  Step 1 — Fix the reserve time: t_res = 0.50 h (day) or 0.75 h (night).
  Step 2 — Determine normal cruising speed (TAS) V_c and cruise fuel flow FF_c (usable gallons per hour) for the planned power setting and altitude.
  Step 3 — Reserve distance: D_res = V_c × t_res.
  Step 4 — Reserve fuel: F_res = FF_c × t_res.
  Step 5 — Total usable fuel at takeoff: F_total = F_taxi + F_trip(first point of intended landing, wind-adjusted) + F_res.
  Step 6 — Compare F_total against usable capacity; if it does not fit, the flight cannot legally be begun as planned.

Worked examples (no wind, for illustration only — substitute the actual airplane's book numbers):

| V_c (KTAS) | FF_c (gal/h) | Day: t=0.50 h → distance / fuel | Night: t=0.75 h → distance / fuel |
|---|---|---|---|
| 120 | 10.0 | 60 NM / 5.0 gal | 90 NM / 7.5 gal |
| 150 | 12.0 | 75 NM / 6.0 gal | 112.5 NM / 9.0 gal |

Arithmetic check: 120 × 0.50 = 60 NM; 120 × 0.75 = 90 NM; 10.0 × 0.50 = 5.0 gal; 10.0 × 0.75 = 7.5 gal; 150 × 0.50 = 75 NM; 150 × 0.75 = 112.5 NM; 12.0 × 0.50 = 6.0 gal; 12.0 × 0.75 = 9.0 gal. Every figure is internally consistent with the 30- and 45-minute thresholds and none exceeds them.

5. RELATED RULES — DO NOT CONFUSE

- § 91.151(b): rotorcraft VFR reserve is 20 minutes. Not applicable to airplanes.
- § 91.167(a)(3): IFR reserve is 45 minutes at normal cruising speed after the first airport of intended landing and, where required, the alternate airport (30 minutes for helicopters). The IFR figure coincidentally equals the VFR night figure, but the IFR rule is a different computation with an alternate-airport component and does not satisfy or replace § 91.151 for a VFR flight.
- § 91.153(a)(5)–(6): a filed VFR flight plan states cruising altitude, true airspeed, point of first intended landing, and estimated elapsed time to that point — the same "first point of intended landing" concept the reserve is measured from.
- Over-the-top or night VFR equipment under § 91.205 / related sections is a separate airworthiness requirement and does not alter the reserve.

6. AUDIT TRAIL

Text verified against three retrievals listed in §2 above (2026 print CFR, 2025 XML CFR, current eCFR), all fetched 2026-11-15, all agreeing word-for-word on the 30-minute and 45-minute figures. Because the answer is a fixed regulatory time, no aircraft-specific performance data, route data, or operator data is needed to state it; performance data enters only at the conversion step in §4, which the operator supplies for the specific airplane.

results.value: 30 minutes by day; 45 minutes by night, each at normal cruising speed

verdict.summary:
TIMING OF INDIVIDUAL BREACH NOTIFICATION UNDER 45 CFR § 164.404(b)

1. CONTROLLING TEXT

45 CFR § 164.404(b) — 'Implementation specification: Timeliness of notification':

"Except as provided in § 164.412, a covered entity shall provide the notification required by paragraph (a) of this section without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach."

45 CFR § 164.404(a)(2) — 'Breaches treated as discovered':

"For purposes of paragraph (a)(1) of this section, §§ 164.406(a), and 164.408(a), a breach shall be treated as discovered by a covered entity as of the first day on which such breach is known to the covered entity, or, by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known to the covered entity. A covered entity shall be deemed to have knowledge of a breach if such breach is known, or by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known, to any person, other than the person committing the breach, who is a workforce member or agent of the covered entity (determined in accordance with the federal common law of agency)."

2. ANSWER — THE THREE POINTS ASKED

(a) Standard (the rule of conduct). Notification must be provided "without unreasonable delay." This is an independent obligation, not a grace period: a covered entity that could reasonably notify sooner must do so, even if the 60-day window has not run.

(b) Outer limit (the backstop). "In no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach." The 60 days are calendar days, counted from the day of discovery; the count is not business days and is not tolled by an ongoing internal investigation. The 60-day figure is a ceiling on permissible delay, never a permitted waiting period.

(c) Triggering event from which the limit runs. "Discovery of a breach," as defined in § 164.404(a)(2): the first day on which the breach is known to the covered entity, or, by exercising reasonable diligence, would have been known to it. Constructive knowledge is imputed: the covered entity is deemed to have knowledge if the breach is known, or by reasonable diligence would have been known, to any person (other than the person committing the breach) who is a workforce member or agent of the covered entity, determined under the federal common law of agency. The clock therefore starts at imputed knowledge, not at the conclusion of the risk assessment or the end of the forensics engagement.

3. CONDITIONS AND QUALIFICATIONS ON THE OUTER LIMIT

- § 164.412 exception. The 60-day limit in § 164.404(b) is expressly subject to § 164.412 (delay for law enforcement purposes). Where § 164.412 applies, notification is delayed for the period specified by a law enforcement official's written statement, and the 60-day ceiling is displaced to that extent. Absent § 164.412, the ceiling is unqualified.
- No size-based variation. Unlike § 164.408(b) (Secretary notice, 500-or-more tier) and § 164.406 (media notice for breaches affecting more than 500 residents of a State or jurisdiction), § 164.404(b) prescribes a single timing rule for individual notice regardless of the number of individuals affected.
- Unsecured PHI only. The duty in § 164.404(a)(1), to which (b) attaches, is triggered by a breach of unsecured protected health information — i.e., PHI that is not rendered unusable, unreadable, or indecipherable to unauthorized persons through a permitted technology or methodology. If the PHI is secured, no § 164.404 notification duty (and therefore no (b) deadline) arises.

4. VALUES THAT MUST NOT BE CONFUSED WITH THE § 164.404(b) DEADLINE

- 90 days: the duration of substitute-notice website posting or toll-free number availability under § 164.404(d)(2)(ii), and the media-notice timing context — not the individual-notice deadline.
- 60 days in § 164.406(b): media notification for breaches affecting more than 500 residents of a State or jurisdiction, running from the same discovery event under § 164.404(a)(2). Same number, different addressee; it is not the individual-notification rule.
- 60 days in § 164.408(b): Secretary notification for breaches involving 500 or more individuals.
The individual-notification answer is: without unreasonable delay, and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery.

5. APPLICATION PROCEDURE (HOW TO FIX THE DATE ON A FILE)

Step 1 — Fix the discovery date. Identify the first day the breach was known, or by reasonable diligence would have been known, to the covered entity or to any workforce member or agent other than the person committing the breach. Record that date as Day 0.

Step 2 — Set the outer-limit date. Day 0 + 60 calendar days. Example: discovery on 1 March gives an outer limit of 30 April in a non-leap year (March has 31 days, so day 60 falls on 30 April).

Step 3 — Test the standard independently. Ask whether notification could reasonably have been given earlier than the outer-limit date; if so, that earlier reasonable date governs, and the 60-day figure provides no protection for the interval between them.

Step 4 — Check for § 164.412. If a law enforcement official has provided the written statement contemplated by § 164.412, document the delay period and the official's statement; otherwise the outer-limit date stands.

Step 5 — Document both dates (Day 0 and the outer-limit date) plus the content elements required by § 164.404(c) in the notification itself, including the date of the breach and the date of discovery, if known.

6. CITATION

45 CFR § 164.404(b), with § 164.404(a)(2) supplying the definition of 'discovered'; § 164.412 supplying the sole express exception to the 60-calendar-day ceiling. Text as published in the current eCFR and the 2025 edition of the CFR (45 CFR part 164, subpart D).

The section's source note ends '...91 FR 1431, Jan. 14, 2026', so the version relied on is the current, in-force text as of the fetch date.

MEASURE (applies to both answers)
Both limits are expressed in PEAK ENVELOPE POWER (PEP), not mean power and not carrier power. PEP is the average power supplied to the antenna transmission line by a transmitter during any period in which the transmitter is producing its maximum power output, taken over a period of time not less than one complete cycle of the RF wave at the highest modulating frequency; the definition resides in § 97.3 (definitions). Note: the exact paragraph number within § 97.3 was not present in the passages I verified, so it is described rather than cited by paragraph.

ASK 1 — GENERAL MAXIMUM TRANSMITTER POWER
§ 97.313(b): 'No station may transmit with a transmitter power exceeding 1.5 kW PEP.'
Answer: 1.5 kW PEP (= 1,500 W PEP). This is the general ceiling for an amateur station, applicable absent a stricter band-, class-, region-, or emission-specific limit elsewhere in § 97.313.

ASK 2 — LOWER LIMIT ON THE 10.10-10.15 MHz SEGMENT
§ 97.313(c): 'No station may transmit with a transmitter power output exceeding 200 W PEP:' and § 97.313(c)(1): 'On the 10.10-10.15 MHz segment'.
Answer: 200 W PEP.

ORDERING / WHICH LIMIT GOVERNS
200 W PEP < 1,500 W PEP, so on 10.10-10.15 MHz (the 30 m band) the paragraph (c)(1) limit controls and the paragraph (b) 1.5 kW ceiling is not reachable. The two figures are consistent: the segment limit is strictly the lower one, which is exactly the relationship the question presupposes.

TEXTUAL DETAIL WORTH FLAGGING
Paragraph (b) speaks of 'transmitter power'; paragraph (c) speaks of 'transmitter power output'. Both are quantified in W PEP. Do not report either as mean power or as DC input power.

OVERLAYS THAT COULD FURTHER REDUCE POWER (not part of the two answers, noted so the answers are not misapplied)
- § 97.313(a): an amateur station must use the minimum transmitter power necessary to carry out the desired communications — a duty independent of, and potentially stricter than, any numeric ceiling.
- § 97.313(j): 10 W PEP transmitter output when transmitting an SS (spread-spectrum) emission type — would override 200 W on this segment for that emission.
- Other band-specific limits in (d)-(m) (1.25 m/23 cm Novice limits, 70 cm restricted areas, 33 cm White Sands, 219-220 MHz, 60 m ERP, 2200 m and 630 m, 76-81 GHz) do not apply to 10.10-10.15 MHz and do not modify either answer.

EDITION STABILITY CHECK
In the 1996 print edition the 200 W PEP figure for 10.10-10.15 MHz appeared in a combined list with 3.675-3.725 MHz, 7.10-7.15 MHz and 21.1-21.2 MHz; in the current text it stands alone in (c)(1) alongside Novice/Technician segments in (c)(2) and the ITU Region 1/3 7.050-7.075 MHz provision in (c)(3). The 200 W PEP value for the 10.10-10.15 MHz segment, and the 1.5 kW PEP general ceiling in (b), are unchanged across those editions.

BOTTOM LINE
General maximum: 1.5 kW PEP (1,500 W PEP).
10.10-10.15 MHz segment maximum: 200 W PEP.

verdict.summary:
CLASS 3 FLAMMABLE LIQUID — FLASH POINT THRESHOLD UNDER 49 CFR § 173.120(a)

1. THE FIGURE AND THE COMPARISON

Governing text (49 CFR § 173.120(a), Flammable liquid), quoted verbatim:

  "For the purpose of this subchapter, a flammable liquid (Class 3) means a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F), or any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging, with the following exceptions: ..."

Threshold: 60 °C (140 °F).

Comparison: NOT MORE THAN — i.e., at or below. Expressed as an inequality:

  flash point ≤ 60 °C (≤ 140 °F)  →  Class 3 flammable liquid
  flash point > 60 °C (> 140 °F)  →  not a Class 3 flammable liquid under this prong

The boundary is inclusive on the upper side: a liquid whose flash point is exactly 60 °C (140 °F) IS a Class 3 flammable liquid. The regulation says "not more than," not "below" and not "less than."

Unit consistency: 60 °C × 9/5 + 32 = 140 °F exactly. The two figures in the regulatory text are an exact conversion of one another; there is no rounding discrepancy at this threshold, and no basis for treating 140 °F as the "real" limit and 60 °C as an approximation (or vice versa). Both are stated in the rule and either may be used to classify.

2. SECOND PRONG OF (a) — ELEVATED TEMPERATURE MATERIALS (do not confuse with the threshold)

The same paragraph captures a second class of material that does not depend on the ≤ 60 °C limit: any material in a liquid phase with a flash point AT OR ABOVE 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation, or transported, at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging. For such a material, the operative comparison is not "≤ 60 °C" but "transport temperature ≥ its own flash point." Note the figure here is 37.8 °C (100 °F), not 38 °C; 100 °F converts to 37.78 °C and the regulation rounds to 37.8. Separately, § 173.120(b)(2) uses 38 °C (100 °F) for the reclassification provision — a different paragraph with a different function. Do not substitute one for the other.

3. EXCEPTIONS THAT OVERRIDE THE ≤ 60 °C RULE (§ 173.120(a)(1)–(5))

A liquid meeting the ≤ 60 °C test is still not Class 3 if it falls in one of these carve-outs:
 (1) it meets one of the definitions in § 173.115 (Division 2.1 flammable gas, 2.2 non-flammable gas, 2.3 poisonous gas);
 (2) it is a mixture in which components with flash point ≥ 60 °C (140 °F) make up at least 99 percent of total volume, and the mixture is not offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point;
 (3) flash point > 35 °C (95 °F) and it does not sustain combustion per ASTM D 4206 or appendix H of part 173;
 (4) flash point > 35 °C (95 °F) and fire point > 100 °C (212 °F) per ISO 2592;
 (5) flash point > 35 °C (95 °F) in a water-miscible solution with water content > 90 percent by mass.

Practical consequence: exceptions (3)–(5) can only bite in the band 35 °C < FP ≤ 60 °C. Below 35 °C (95 °F) the carve-outs do not apply, and a liquid with FP ≤ 35 °C is Class 3 on the flash point alone (subject only to exception (1)).

4. ADJACENT BOUNDARY — COMBUSTIBLE LIQUID (§ 173.120(b)(1))

  "... a combustible liquid means any liquid that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class specified in this subchapter and has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F)."

The two definitions tile cleanly at 60 °C (140 °F): ≤ 60 °C is Class 3; > 60 °C is outside Class 3 and, up to 93 °C (200 °F), is a combustible liquid. Exactly 60 °C belongs to Class 3, not to the combustible range. (Note (b)(2) allows a Class 3 liquid with flash point at or above 38 °C (100 °F) to be reclassed as a combustible liquid where it meets no other hazard class definition, but that reclassification is unavailable for vessel or aircraft transport except where other means of transport is impracticable, and is unavailable for elevated-temperature materials.)

5. MEASUREMENT BASIS — WHAT "FLASH POINT" MEANS HERE (§ 173.120(c))

The 60 °C (140 °F) figure is a closed-cup flash point. § 173.120(c)(1) prescribes the test:
 - (c)(1)(i) homogeneous, single-phase liquid with viscosity < 45 S.U.S. at 38 °C (100 °F) that does not form a surface film under test: ASTM D 56 (Tag Closed Cup), ASTM D 3278 (Small Scale Closed-Cup), or ASTM D 3828 (Small Scale Closed Tester).
 - (c)(1)(ii) any other liquid: ASTM D 93 (Pensky-Martens Closed Cup; Method B for cutback asphalt), ASTM D 3278, ISO 1516, or the further methods listed in that subparagraph.
An open-cup result is not a valid basis for the § 173.120(a) classification, and a closed-cup result obtained by a method outside (c)(1) is not the regulatory measurement. All methods are incorporated by reference under § 171.7.

6. VERSION STABILITY

The 60 °C (140 °F) threshold and the "not more than" wording are identical in the 2018, 2023, 2024 and 2025 printed editions of 49 CFR and in the current eCFR text of § 173.120(a). The answer does not depend on which in-force edition is cited. The surrounding exceptions have been stable across those editions as well (the 2018 text shows exceptions (1)–(5) in the same form).

7. WORKED BOUNDARY CHECK

  FP = 25 °C (77 °F)   → ≤ 60 °C → Class 3 (exceptions (3)–(5) unavailable below 35 °C)
  FP = 35 °C (95 °F)   → ≤ 60 °C → Class 3; exceptions (3)–(5) keyed to "greater than 35 °C" are not triggered
  FP = 45 °C (113 °F)  → ≤ 60 °C → Class 3 unless it fails to sustain combustion / has fire point > 100 °C per ISO 2592 / is > 90% water-miscible
  FP = 60 °C (140 °F)  → ≤ 60 °C → Class 3 (boundary is inclusive; "not more than")
  FP = 60.5 °C (141 °F) → > 60 °C → not Class 3 under (a); evaluate as combustible liquid under (b) if it meets no other hazard class
  FP = 93 °C (200 °F)  → not Class 3; at the upper edge of the combustible range

8. INTERNATIONAL NOTE (context only — not the answer to the question asked)

The UN Model Regulations, IMDG Code and IATA DGR likewise set the flammable-liquid cut-off at 60 °C closed cup, so the DOT figure is aligned internationally at the transport-classification level. GHS hazard categorization subdivides differently (Category 1 ≤ 23 °C, Category 2 > 23 °C and ≤ 60 °C, Category 3 > 60 °C and ≤ 93 °C) and should not be conflated with the 49 CFR Class 3 / combustible-liquid split, which places everything at or below 60 °C in a single Class 3.

BOTTOM LINE: Under 49 CFR § 173.120(a), a Class 3 flammable liquid is a liquid with a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F) — at or below 60 °C / 140 °F, closed cup — subject to the five listed exceptions and to the separate elevated-temperature provision for liquids with flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) transported at or above their flash point in bulk packaging.

verdict.summary:
RFC 1918 ("Address Allocation for Private Internets", Rekhter et al., February 1996, BCP 5), Section 3 "Private Address Space", reserves exactly three blocks of IPv4 address space for private internets. Verbatim from the RFC:

  "The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) has reserved the
   following three blocks of the IP address space for private internets:

   10.0.0.0        -   10.255.255.255  (10/8 prefix)
   172.16.0.0      -   172.31.255.255  (172.16/12 prefix)
   192.168.0.0     -   192.168.255.255 (192.168/16 prefix)"

TABLE OF THE THREE BLOCKS

| # | RFC 1918 name   | Range (first - last address)     | CIDR / prefix  | Prefix len | Host bits | Addresses |
|---|-----------------|----------------------------------|----------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| 1 | "24-bit block"  | 10.0.0.0   - 10.255.255.255      | 10.0.0.0/8     | /8        | 24        | 16,777,216 (2^24) |
| 2 | "20-bit block"  | 172.16.0.0 - 172.31.255.255      | 172.16.0.0/12  | /12       | 20        | 1,048,576 (2^20)  |
| 3 | "16-bit block"  | 192.168.0.0 - 192.168.255.255    | 192.168.0.0/16 | /16       | 16        | 65,536 (2^16)     |

Total reserved: 16,777,216 + 1,048,576 + 65,536 = 17,891,328 addresses, i.e. 2^24 + 2^20 + 2^16 out of 2^32 = 4,294,967,296, approximately 0.4166% of the IPv4 unicast space.

Note on the RFC's own naming: RFC 1918 labels these the "24-bit", "20-bit" and "16-bit" blocks. Those labels count HOST bits, not prefix bits — 32 - 8 = 24, 32 - 12 = 20, 32 - 16 = 16 — so they are consistent with, not contradictory to, the /8, /12 and /16 prefix lengths above. RFC 1918 also notes (pre-CIDR terms) that the first block is a single class A network number, the second is a set of 16 contiguous class B network numbers, and the third is a set of 256 contiguous class C network numbers.

INTERNAL CONSISTENCY CHECKS ON THE NUMBERS ABOVE

1. Prefix length vs. address count: /8 -> 2^(32-8) = 2^24 = 16,777,216. /12 -> 2^20 = 1,048,576. /16 -> 2^16 = 65,536. Each count is exactly the size of the stated range.
2. The /12 block's span: 172.16.0.0 through 172.31.255.255 covers second-octet values 16..31 inclusive = 16 values, each contributing 256 x 256 = 65,536 addresses: 16 x 65,536 = 1,048,576 = 2^20. Consistent with /12.
3. No block overlaps another (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16 are disjoint), and the sum 17,891,328 does not exceed the total IPv4 space 4,294,967,296.

COMMON MISQUOTES TO AVOID (relevant to any implementation that hard-codes these)

- The middle block is 172.16.0.0/12, NOT 172.16.0.0/16. It ends at 172.31.255.255, not 172.16.255.255. If a config or parser uses 172.16.0.0/16 it will wrongly treat 172.17.0.0 - 172.31.255.255 as public.
- The first block is 10.0.0.0/8, not 10.0.0.0/24 or 10.0.0.0/16.
- The third block is 192.168.0.0/16, not 192.168.0.0/24.

SCOPE / DISAMBIGUATION (not part of the answer, but guards against conflating ranges)

- RFC 1918 private space is only these three blocks. Other special-use IPv4 ranges are NOT RFC 1918 private addresses and must not be merged into this list, notably: 169.254.0.0/16 link-local (RFC 3927), 127.0.0.0/8 loopback (RFC 1122), 100.64.0.0/10 shared address space / CGN (RFC 6598), 0.0.0.0/8, 224.0.0.0/4 multicast, 240.0.0.0/4 reserved, 192.0.2.0/24 TEST-NET-1, 198.51.100.0/24 TEST-NET-2, 203.0.113.0/24 TEST-NET-3, 198.18.0.0/15 benchmarking.
- The set has not been extended. RFC 6319 ("Designating Additional Private IPv4 Address Space", July 2011, Informational) opens by restating the same three — "[RFC1918] sets aside three blocks of IPv4 address space for use in private networks: 192.168.0.0/16, 172.16.0.0/12 and 10.0.0.0/8" — and concludes that allocating additional private space has severe problems; it makes no recommendation to add a fourth block. So the RFC 1918 answer remains the complete and current answer.

ANSWER, CONDENSED

RFC 1918 reserves these three blocks for private internets:
  1. 10.0.0.0/8      (10.0.0.0 - 10.255.255.255)
  2. 172.16.0.0/12   (172.16.0.0 - 172.31.255.255)
  3. 192.168.0.0/16  (192.168.0.0 - 192.168.255.255)

Source: RFC 1918, Section 3, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918.txt; corroborated by RFC 6319, Section 1.

verdict.summary:
## 1. Answer (regulatory text)

40 CFR § 50.19 (source note [80 FR 65452, Oct. 26, 2015]; still the codified text in the current eCFR, as fetched):

> (a) The level of the national 8-hour primary ambient air quality standard for ozone (O3) is **0.070 parts per million (ppm), daily maximum 8-hour average**, measured by a reference method based on appendix D to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter or an equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.
>
> (b) The 8-hour primary O3 ambient air quality standard is **met at an ambient air quality monitoring site when the 3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average O3 concentration is less than or equal to 0.070 ppm**, as determined in accordance with appendix U to this part.

## 2. Ask 1 — Level of the national 8-hour primary O3 standard

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Level | **0.070 ppm** |
| Equivalent | 70 ppb (1 ppm = 1,000 ppb) |
| Metric it is expressed on | daily maximum 8-hour average |
| Pollutant form | O3 |
| Standard type | primary (health-based); § 50.19(c) sets the secondary at the identical 0.070 ppm |
| Measurement basis | reference method per appendix D, designated per part 53, or equivalent method per part 53 |
| Regulatory citation | 40 CFR § 50.19(a) |

Notes a reviewer must not get wrong:

- The level is **0.070 ppm, not 0.075 ppm and not 0.08 ppm**. Those are superseded standards: § 50.15 sets 0.075 ppm (2008, with its own form under appendix P), and the 1997 0.08 ppm 8-hour standard is revoked. The current 2015 standard is § 50.19 at 0.070 ppm; the 2024 review action (89 FR 105785, Dec. 27, 2024) amended appendix U, not the 0.070 ppm level.
- The level is expressed **in ppm, not µg/m³**. Do not convert to mass concentration for purposes of applying this standard; the regulatory comparison is ppm (reported at 1 ppb = 0.001 ppm resolution).
- The primary and secondary 8-hour O3 standards are numerically identical (0.070 ppm) but are separate standards with separate attainment determinations under § 50.19(b) and § 50.19(d).

## 3. Ask 2 — When the standard is met at a monitoring site

The standard is met when the **design value** — the 3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average O3 concentration — is **≤ 0.070 ppm**, computed per appendix U to part 50. Appendix U § 1 states this and adds the validity rule.

### 3.1 Computation procedure

1. **Daily maximum 8-hour average.** For each day of the O3 monitoring season, compute the running 8-hour averages from valid hourly O3 data and take the highest; that day's value is the daily maximum 8-hour average, expressed to three decimal places in ppm (1 ppb). Appendix D/appendix U convention: an 8-hour average is valid only if the hourly data are sufficiently complete (at least 75% of the hourly values in the 8-hour period, i.e., 6 of 8 hours); days failing that are not valid daily maxima. (This hourly-validity detail is the appendix D/U convention rather than text quoted above — cite appendix D/U § 3 when writing it into a formal document.)
2. **Annual fourth-highest.** For each year, rank that year's valid daily maximum 8-hour averages and take the **fourth-highest**. (Not the fourth-highest *exceedance*; the fourth-highest daily maximum.)
3. **Three-year average.** Average the annual fourth-highest values from three consecutive years.
4. **Truncate, do not round.** Truncate the 3-year average to three decimal places (ppm). Appendix U Example 1 is explicit: 0.065666 ppm is "truncated to 0.065 ppm."
5. **Compare.** If the truncated design value is **≤ 0.070 ppm**, the standard is met at that site; if **> 0.070 ppm**, it is not met.

### 3.2 Data-completeness / validity rule (appendix U)

- A design value **greater than** 0.070 ppm is **always** considered valid (incomplete data cannot be used to excuse an exceedance).
- A design value **less than or equal to** 0.070 ppm is valid only if minimum data completeness is met for the 3-year period: valid daily maximum 8-hour averages on **at least 90% of the days within the O3 monitoring season, on average, over the 3 years**, with a **minimum of 75% of season days in any one year**.
- Meteorological or ambient data may be used to show that missing days were not conducive to concentrations above the level of the standard; such missing days are counted toward completeness (appendix U). Data affected by exceptional events may be excluded under the separate Exceptional Events Rule (40 CFR § 50.14).
- The O3 monitoring season is the season specified for the state in appendix D to part 50; completeness is measured against season days, not calendar days.

### 3.3 Worked example (reproduced from appendix U Example 1, arithmetic re-verified)

| Year | % valid season days | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | **4th highest** | 5th |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2014 | 100 | 0.082 | 0.080 | 0.075 | **0.069** | 0.068 |
| 2015 | 96 | 0.074 | 0.073 | 0.065 | **0.062** | 0.060 |
| 2016 | 98 | 0.070 | 0.069 | 0.067 | **0.066** | 0.060 |
| Average | 98 | | | | **0.065** | |

(0.069 + 0.062 + 0.066) / 3 = 0.197 / 3 = 0.0656667 → truncated to **0.065 ppm**. 0.065 ≤ 0.070, so the site **meets** the primary (and secondary) O3 NAAQS. Completeness: 98% average ≥ 90%, and no year below 75% — so the design value is valid.

### 3.4 Practical consequences of the form

- A site can record daily maxima above 0.070 ppm in all three years and still meet the standard, because the form uses the **fourth-highest** day of each year — up to three exceedance-level days per year are absorbed by the form.
- Because the comparison uses a **truncated** 3-decimal design value, a computed average of, e.g., 0.0709 ppm truncates to 0.070 ppm and **meets** the standard; the same average rounded would read 0.071 and appear to fail. Truncation is therefore outcome-determinative near the threshold and must be applied as written.
- A site with a valid design value ≤ 0.070 ppm but sub-90%/sub-75% completeness **cannot** be treated as meeting the standard on that basis; the correct statement is that the data are insufficient to determine the site as meeting the standard.

## 4. Scope, provenance and limits

- Everything above is drawn from the codified text of § 50.19 and appendix U as fetched from eCFR (sha256 29cc1e46ed44), the part 50 index (sha256 2bd487ed7945), Cornell LII (sha256 7ec868d9bf45) and the 2025 print of appendix U (sha256 89e46e649721). All sources agree on 0.070 ppm and on the ≤ 0.070 ppm / 3-year-average-of-annual-fourth-highest form.
- This is a statement of the regulatory definition only. It is **not** an attainment determination for any actual monitoring site; that requires the site's three years of quality-assured daily maximum 8-hour averages, its appendix D season, and its completeness record.
- No site-specific data, permit application, or project documentation was needed or used, and none of the above depends on such data.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER — 29 C.F.R. § 825.200(a) (FMLA entitlement, military caregiver leave excluded)

1) AMOUNT: 12 workweeks.
An eligible employee's FMLA leave entitlement is limited to a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period. 29 C.F.R. § 825.200(a); 29 U.S.C. § 2612(a)(1). The 12 workweeks is one combined pool for all five qualifying reasons listed in § 825.200(a)(1)–(5) — birth/care of newborn; placement for adoption or foster care/care of newly placed child; care of a spouse, son, daughter, or parent with a serious health condition; the employee's own serious health condition; and qualifying exigency arising from a covered family member's covered active duty — not 12 weeks per reason, per condition, or per family member. The regulation's words are 'for any one, or more, of the following reasons,' i.e., the cap is aggregate.

2) PERIOD: 12 months — 'any 12-month period,' measured by one of four employer-selected methods.
The entitlement is 12 workweeks during any 12-month period. The employer chooses which 12-month period applies and must apply it consistently and uniformly to all employees. § 825.200(b) permits only these four methods:
  (b)(1) the calendar year;
  (b)(2) any fixed 12-month leave year — e.g., a fiscal year, a year required by State law, or a year starting on the employee's anniversary date;
  (b)(3) the 12-month period measured forward from the date any employee's first FMLA leave under § 825.200(a) begins; or
  (b)(4) a 'rolling' 12-month period measured backward from the date the employee uses any FMLA leave under § 825.200(a).
No fifth method is permitted; the regulation says the employer is 'permitted to choose any one of the following methods.'

How the choice changes what the employee can actually take (§ 825.200(c)):
  • Fixed methods, (b)(1) and (b)(2): the employee is entitled to up to 12 workweeks at any time within the fixed period, so an employee may take 12 workweeks at the end of one fixed year and another 12 workweeks at the start of the next — up to 24 workweeks across a short span straddling the boundary. That is lawful under these methods.
  • Forward method, (b)(3): 12 workweeks during the 12-month period beginning on the first date FMLA leave is taken; the next 12-month period begins the first time FMLA leave is taken after the prior period is complete.
  • Rolling method, (b)(4): each time the employee takes FMLA leave, the remaining entitlement is whatever balance of the 12 workweeks has not been used during the immediately preceding 12 months. This method prevents end-of-year/start-of-year stacking.
Administration of the choice: the employer must select a method and apply it uniformly; a change of method requires notice (a 60-day period under § 825.200(d)), and during the transition the employee may use the option that provides the most beneficial outcome to that employee, with the selected option implemented at the end of the 60 days. Where no method has been validly selected, the option most beneficial to the employee governs.

3) COVERED-SERVICEMEMBER LEAVE — CARVED OUT, NOT COUNTED HERE.
The 26-workweek military caregiver entitlement is expressly excluded from this answer. § 825.200(a) opens 'Except in the case of leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness,' and that entitlement lives in § 825.200(f)–(g) and § 825.127(e): 26 workweeks during a single 12-month period measured forward from the first day the employee takes such leave, with unused caregiver weeks forfeited at the end of that period (§ 825.127(e)(1)), and a combined 26-workweek cap for all FMLA reasons during that single period (§ 825.200(g)). Those provisions are noted only to mark the boundary of this answer; they do not change the 12-workweek/12-month answer above for the five § 825.200(a) reasons. (The regulation's illustration — e.g., 16 weeks of caregiver leave plus 10 weeks of newborn care within the single period, but never more than 12 weeks of newborn care — belongs to that excluded caregiver context and is not an entitlement figure under this answer.)

4) CONVERTING '12 WORKWEEKS' TO HOURS (for tracking and intermittent use).
The unit of measure is the employee's own workweek, not a fixed 40-hour week. 12 workweeks = 12 × the number of hours in the employee's normal scheduled workweek:
  • 40 hrs/week → 480 hours
  • 37.5 hrs/week → 450 hours
  • 20 hrs/week (part-time) → 240 hours
For part-time employees and for leave taken on a reduced schedule, entitlement is prorated to the employee's normal schedule. § 825.205(b)(1); § 825.205(a)–(b). Airline flight crew employees are subject to the special calculation in § 825.802 (hours-worked/credited-hours basis) rather than a literal 12 × weekly-hours figure.

5) COUNTING RULES THAT AFFECT HOW THE 12 WORKWEEKS IS CONSUMED.
  • A holiday falling inside a week taken as FMLA leave does not reduce the charge: the week counts as a week of FMLA leave. § 825.200(h).
  • Where leave is taken in increments of less than a week, a holiday in that week has no effect and the employee is charged only for the leave actually taken. § 825.200(h).
  • Intermittent leave and reduced-schedule leave are charged in the actual increments used and reduce the remaining 12-week balance proportionally. § 825.205(a)–(b).
  • Periods when the employer's operations have ceased do not count against the entitlement. § 825.200 (closing text, cross-referencing § 825.205).

6) SCOPE NOTES (limits of this answer, not additional entitlements).
  • 'Eligible employee' is taken as satisfied — the 12-month/1,250-hour test and worksite/50-employee coverage are assumed met and are not analyzed here. 29 U.S.C. § 2611(2); § 825.110.
  • The 12 workweeks is the statutory entitlement floor/ceiling combination: an employer may provide more leave by policy, agreement, or CBA, but any excess is not FMLA leave and carries no FMLA reinstatement right.
  • FMLA leave is unpaid unless the employer's policy or a CBA provides otherwise; substitution of accrued paid leave (§ 825.207) changes the pay, not the 12-workweek amount.
  • Bonding leave for birth or placement has an additional outer time limit: the entitlement expires at the end of the 12-month period beginning on the date of birth or placement, even if the employer's § 825.200(b) method would otherwise allow later use. § 825.120(a)(2); § 825.121.
  • Where both spouses are employed by the same covered employer, a combined 12-week limit applies to leave for birth/placement/child care and for care of a parent. §§ 825.120(b), 825.121(b), 825.201(b).
  • This is a single-employer entitlement determination; multi-employer and successor-employer scenarios are out of scope.

BOTTOM LINE: 12 workweeks of FMLA leave, taken during a 12-month period, with the employer selecting one of the four § 825.200(b) methods (calendar year, fixed 12-month leave year, forward-measured from first FMLA leave, or rolling backward from use) and applying it uniformly — the 12 workweeks being a single combined entitlement for all § 825.200(a) reasons and excluding the 26-workweek covered-servicemember entitlement under § 825.200(f)–(g).

verdict.summary:
RFC 5321 (October 2008), Section 4.5.3.1 — Size Limits and Minimums

Normative text:

4.5.3.1.5. Reply Line
The maximum total length of a reply line including the reply code and the <CRLF> is 512 octets. More information may be conveyed through multiple-line replies.

4.5.3.1.6. Text Line
The maximum total length of a text line including the <CRLF> is 1000 octets (not counting the leading dot duplicated for transparency). This number may be increased by the use of SMTP Service Extensions.

Direct answers:

1. SMTP text line — maximum total length: 1000 octets. This is the total SMTP line length including the terminating <CRLF> (2 octets), i.e. at most 998 octets of line content before the CRLF. The extra leading dot inserted for transparency (dot-stuffing) is not counted, so a dot-stuffed line can be 1001 octets on the wire while still conforming. The limit may be raised by SMTP service extensions.

2. SMTP reply line — maximum total length: 512 octets. This includes the 3-octet reply code, the separator (a hyphen '-' on non-final lines of a multiline reply or a space on the final line), any reply text, and the terminating <CRLF>. Multiline replies do not increase the per-line limit; each line of a multiline reply is a reply line subject to the same 512-octet maximum.

What the counts include:
- Both are octet counts, not character counts. Section 4.5.3.1 specifies lengths "in octets where absolute lengths, rather than character counts, are intended."
- Both maxima include the terminating <CRLF> pair (2 octets).
- The text-line count excludes only the leading dot duplicated for transparency; the original content dot, if any, is part of the content and counts.
- The reply-line count includes the reply code, the code/text separator, the reply text, and the CRLF. Per Section 4.2, the space following the reply code is considered part of the text.
- Neither count includes lower-layer (TCP/IP) framing; these are SMTP line lengths.

Related limits in the same section, for context only: command line 512 octets including the command word and <CRLF>; local-part 64 octets; domain 255 octets; path 256 octets; message content at least 64K octets. The RFC 5321bis drafts (e.g. -43) retain the 1000-octet text-line and 512-octet reply-line limits.

verdict.summary:
49 CFR § 395.3(a) — property-carrying CMV, baseline rule (no § 395.1 exceptions applied)

ANSWERS

| # | Question | Value | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Consecutive hours off duty required before driving | 10 consecutive hours off duty | § 395.3(a)(1) |
| 2 | Consecutive-hour threshold after which the driver may no longer drive | 14 consecutive hours after coming on duty | § 395.3(a)(2) |
| 3 | Total hours that may be driven within that period | 11 hours total driving | § 395.3(a)(3)(i) |

CONTROLLING TEXT (verbatim, current eCFR; identical in the 2023 and 2025 CFR annual editions)

§ 395.3 Maximum driving time for property-carrying vehicles.

"(a) Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1, no motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, unless the driver complies with the following requirements:

(1) Start of work shift. A driver may not drive without first taking 10 consecutive hours off duty;

(2) 14-hour period. A driver may not drive after a period of 14 consecutive hours after coming on-duty following 10 consecutive hours off-duty.

(3) Driving time and interruptions of driving periods — (i) Driving time. A driver may drive a total of 11 hours during the period specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section.

(ii) Interruption of driving time. Except for drivers who qualify for either of the short-haul exceptions in § 395.1(e)(1) or (2), driving is not permitted if more than 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status. A consecutive 30-minute interruption of driving status may be satisfied either by off-duty, sleeper berth or on-duty not driving time or by a combination of off-duty, sleeper berth and on-duty not driving time."

Source citations: 49 CFR § 395.3(a) (eCFR current, fetched 2026-11-15); CFR 2025 title 49 vol. 5 § 395.3 (govinfo PDF); CFR 2023 title 49 vol. 5 § 395.3 (govinfo XML). Source note line: "[76 FR 81188, Dec. 27, 2011, as amended at 78 FR 58485, Sept. 24, 2013; 78 FR 64181, Oct. 28, 2013; 84 FR 48081, Sept. 12, 2019; 85 FR 33452, June 1, 2020]" — the last amendment (June 1, 2020) is the one that produced the current (a)(3)(ii) 30-minute-interruption wording; it did not change the 10/14/11 figures.

HOW EACH NUMBER IS READ OFF THE TEXT

Ask 1 — 10 hours. § 395.3(a)(1) is a precondition on driving: no driving until 10 consecutive hours off duty have been taken. "Consecutive" is explicit; the 10 hours cannot be assembled from scattered shorter breaks under the baseline rule (see sleeper-berth split below for the one regulatory route to an equivalent). "Off duty" includes off-duty time and sleeper-berth time; § 395.1(g)(1)(i)(E) confirms that the equivalent of at least 10 consecutive hours off duty can be accumulated under the split provisions.

Ask 2 — 14 hours. § 395.3(a)(2) bars driving "after a period of 14 consecutive hours after coming on-duty following 10 consecutive hours off-duty." Precision point the wording of the question does not capture: this is a 14-consecutive-hour elapsed-time window measured from the moment the driver comes on duty, not 14 accumulated hours of on-duty time. Off-duty time taken inside the window (other than a qualifying § 395.1(g) sleeper-berth/off-duty pair) does not pause or extend the 14-hour clock; a two-hour off-duty lunch inside the window consumes two of the 14 hours. The 14-hour figure answers the question as asked (the threshold at which driving must stop), but it must not be operated as an on-duty accumulator.

Ask 3 — 11 hours. § 395.3(a)(3)(i) caps total driving at 11 hours "during the period specified in paragraph (a)(2)" — i.e., inside the same 14-hour window. The 11 hours need not be consecutive; it is a cumulative cap. Because the 11 is contained in the 14, and because a 30-minute interruption is required once 8 cumulative driving hours have elapsed, the practical structure inside the window is: drive up to 8 cumulative hours, take at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption (off duty, sleeper berth, on-duty-not-driving, or any combination), then continue up to the 11-hour total, all of which must be completed before the 14th hour after coming on duty.

ADJACENT LIMITS IN THE SAME SECTION THAT ARE NOT ANSWERS TO THESE THREE ASKS

Do not substitute these for any of the three values above:
- § 395.3(a)(3)(ii): the 8-hour/30-minute interruption rule. It bounds how the 11 hours are distributed but does not change the 11, the 14, or the 10.
- § 395.3(b)(1)–(2): 60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days (carrier not operating every day) or 70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days (carrier operating every day). These are separate rolling on-duty ceilings, not the driving window; the request does not ask about them.
- § 395.3(c)(1)–(2): a 7- or 8-day period may end with the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours (the restart). Also not asked.

WORKED APPLICATION (arithmetic consistency check)

Driver takes 10 consecutive hours off duty, coming on duty at 06:00.
- Driving window closes at 06:00 + 14 h = 20:00. No driving after 20:00 regardless of how few driving hours have been used.
- Maximum driving inside the window: 11 hours, so 11 <= 14, satisfied. A driver who drives 11 hours starting at 06:00 finishes at 17:00 and may not drive again until a new 10-consecutive-hour off-duty period is completed and a new window opens.
- The 30-minute interruption is triggered when cumulative driving reaches 8 hours; 8 <= 11, so the trigger is always reachable before the cap is exhausted. Example: driving 06:00–14:00 (8 h) requires at least 30 consecutive minutes of non-driving before any further driving; after that interruption the driver has 3 driving hours left (11 - 8 = 3) and 6 window hours left (20:00 - 14:30 = 5.5 h after the break), so the binding constraint at that point is the 11-hour cap, not the 14-hour window.

SCOPE — WHAT THESE NUMBERS DO NOT COVER

§ 395.3(a) opens with "Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1." The three figures above are the baseline. They are displaced or modified in at least the following cases, and a driver in one of them should not be advised on the 10/14/11 figures alone:
- Short-haul exceptions, § 395.1(e)(1) and (e)(2): drivers who qualify are exempt from the § 395.3(a)(3)(ii) 30-minute interruption rule (and other recordkeeping/duty-status requirements), which changes the shape of the day though not the 10/14/11 baseline caps where those still apply.
- Adverse driving conditions, § 395.1(b)(2): permits up to 2 additional hours of driving beyond the 11-hour and 14-hour limits when adverse conditions were not known before dispatch, followed by a required 10 consecutive hours off duty (property-carrying).
- Sleeper berth, § 395.1(g)(1): a driver may accumulate the equivalent of at least 10 consecutive hours off duty using not more than two periods of sleeper-berth time or a combination of off-duty and sleeper-berth time, provided neither period is shorter than 2 consecutive hours, one period is at least 7 consecutive hours in the sleeper berth, the two total at least 10 hours, and the driving time before and after each rest period when added together does not exceed 11 hours under § 395.3(a)(3) and does not violate the 14-hour limit under § 395.3(a)(2); the 14-hour window does not include those qualifying rest periods. This is the principal lawful way a driver's day departs from a plain 10/14/11 reading.
- Alaska, § 395.1(b)(1): § 395.3(a) and (b) do not apply to drivers in Alaska; the Alaska property-carrying limits are 15 hours following 10 consecutive hours off duty, no driving after being on duty 20 hours or more following 10 consecutive hours off duty, plus 70/80-hour limits.
- Passenger-carrying vehicles are governed by § 395.5, not § 395.3: 10 hours driving following 8 consecutive hours off duty, and no driving after 15 hours on duty following 8 consecutive hours off duty. The numbers in this answer must not be applied to passenger-carrying operations.

VERSION / JURISDICTION NOTE

The three figures are stable across the current eCFR text and the 2023 and 2025 CFR annual editions, so no version conflict affects this answer. The text is the U.S. federal rule (FMCSA, 49 CFR subtitle B, chapter III, subchapter B, part 395, subpart A). Canadian and Mexican hours-of-service regimes are different instruments and are not addressed here.

verdict.summary:
LEGAL ANSWER — 12 C.F.R. § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) (Regulation Z)

I. Question presented
Under 12 C.F.R. § 1026.23(a)(3)(i), until when may a consumer exercise the right to rescind a covered credit transaction, and when does that right expire if the required notice or material disclosures are never delivered?

II. Short answer
A. Ordinary case — notice and material disclosures delivered. The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following the last of three events: (1) consummation of the transaction; (2) delivery of the notice required by § 1026.23(b); and (3) delivery of all material disclosures. The last event controls. If the notice or the material disclosures are delivered after consummation, the three-business-day period runs from that later delivery, not from consummation.
B. Never-delivered case. If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind expires 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first. The 3-year period is an outer limit, not a guaranteed minimum; a transfer of all of the consumer's interest or a sale can terminate the right earlier. Certain administrative proceedings may extend the period under section 125(f) of the Act.

III. Governing text
Section 1026.23(a)(3)(i) provides:
(3)(i) The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last. If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first. In the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act.
Section 1026.23(a)(3)(ii) provides:
For purposes of this paragraph (a)(3), the term material disclosures means the required disclosures of the annual percentage rate, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, the payment schedule, and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g).

IV. Analysis
1. Three triggering events, and the last one controls. The regulation identifies consummation, delivery of the § 1026.23(b) rescission notice, and delivery of all material disclosures. The period does not start until all three have occurred. Official Interpretation, Paragraph 23(a)(3), comment 1.i, states that the period runs for 3 business days from the last of those three events. Comment 1.ii illustrates: if a transaction is consummated on Friday, June 1, and the disclosures and rescission notice were given on Thursday, May 31, the period expires at midnight of the third business day after June 1, which is Tuesday, June 5; if the disclosures and consummation occur on Friday, June 1, and the rescission notice is given on Monday, June 4, the period expires at midnight of the third business day after June 4, which is Thursday, June 7. The notice need not be given before consummation; if it is given later, the period runs from that later date (Official Interpretation, Paragraph 23(b)(1), comment 4).
2. Counting the third business day. The event day is not counted; count forward from the day after the last event. For rescission, business day is defined in § 1026.2(a)(6) as all calendar days except Sundays and the legal public holidays specified in 5 U.S.C. § 6103(a); Saturdays count. If the third business day would be a Sunday or a listed federal holiday, the period runs to the next day that is a business day. The period ends at midnight.
3. How the consumer exercises the right. Under the official interpretation to Paragraph 23(a)(3), comment 1.ii.B, the consumer must place the rescission notice in the mail, file it for telegraphic transmission, or deliver it to the creditor's place of business within the period. The regulation's focus is on dispatch or delivery within the period, not on the creditor's receipt after the period. A creditor should therefore preserve evidence of the date the consumer sent or delivered the notice.
4. Material disclosures are a defined set. Section 1026.23(a)(3)(ii) defines material disclosures as the annual percentage rate, finance charge, amount financed, total of payments, payment schedule, and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g). If any required item in that set is not delivered, the all-material-disclosures trigger has not occurred.
5. The never-delivered rule. The condition in the second sentence is disjunctive: if the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered. Failure to deliver the rescission notice, or failure to deliver all material disclosures, is enough to move the transaction into the extended rule. The right then expires at the earliest of: (a) 3 years after consummation; (b) transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property; or (c) sale of the property. The 3-year date is measured from consummation, not from the date delivery was due or refused. A sale or transfer of all interest within the 3 years ends the right earlier.
6. Delivery versus receipt. The regulation uses delivery, not receipt. In a compliance file, the operative question is when the notice and all material disclosures were delivered to the consumer. If the creditor cannot establish delivery, a court or regulator may treat the item as not delivered and apply the 3-year/transfer/sale rule. This is an evidentiary risk, not a different legal standard.
7. Exempt transactions and refinancings. The timing rule presupposes that a rescission right exists. Section 1026.23(f) exempts, among others, a residential mortgage transaction; a refinancing or consolidation by the same creditor of credit already secured by the consumer's principal dwelling, except to the extent the new amount financed exceeds the unpaid principal balance, earned unpaid finance charge, and amounts attributed solely to refinancing or consolidation costs; a transaction in which a state agency is the creditor; certain subsequent advances where the notice and all material disclosures were given; and certain renewals of optional insurance premiums. If the transaction is exempt, the periods above do not create a rescission right.
8. Administrative proceedings. The last sentence of § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) extends the rescission period in certain administrative proceedings in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act. That extension is separate from the two rules above and should be checked if an administrative enforcement proceeding is involved.

V. Practical application
Step 1. Confirm the transaction is covered and not exempt under § 1026.23(f).
Step 2. Identify the last of: consummation; delivery of the § 1026.23(b) notice; delivery of all material disclosures.
Step 3. If all three occurred, count three business days forward from the day after the last event, using the rescission definition of business day (Saturdays count; Sundays and listed federal holidays do not). The right ends at midnight of the third business day.
Step 4. If the notice or any material disclosure was never delivered, do not use the three-business-day date. Use the earliest of: three years after consummation; transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property; sale of the property.
Step 5. Calendar and document both dates, and preserve delivery evidence. If a transfer or sale occurs, calendar that earlier termination date.

VI. Bottom line for the two asks
Ask 1 — ordinary case: midnight of the third business day following the last of consummation, delivery of the required rescission notice, and delivery of all material disclosures. Numeric period: 3 business days.
Ask 2 — never-delivered case: 3 years after consummation, or earlier upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property or sale of the property, whichever occurs first. Numeric outer limit: 3 years.

VII. Sources
12 C.F.R. § 1026.23(a)(3)(i), current eCFR text (fetched 2026-11-15; sha256 5e060cc324e9); CFPB Regulation Z pages for § 1026.23 and Official Interpretation, Paragraph 23(a)(3), including comments 1.i and 1.ii (2020-12-28 and current versions). This answer is limited to federal Regulation Z; state law may provide different or additional rescission rights.

Conversion basis used: 1 Sv = 100 rem (1 rem = 0.01 Sv). 5/100 = 0.05; 15/100 = 0.15; 50/100 = 0.5. These agree with the parenthetical SI values printed in the regulation itself.

2. VERBATIM REGULATORY TEXT (the controlling language, quoted from the eCFR/GovInfo copies of § 20.1201)

"(a) The licensee shall control the occupational dose to individual adults, except for planned special exposures under § 20.1206, to the following dose limits.
(1) An annual limit, which is the more limiting of—
(i) The total effective dose equivalent being equal to 5 rems (0.05 Sv); or
(ii) The sum of the deep-dose equivalent and the committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens of the eye being equal to 50 rems (0.5 Sv).
(2) The annual limits to the lens of the eye, to the skin of the whole body, and to the skin of the extremities, which are:
(i) A lens dose equivalent of 15 rems (0.15 Sv), and
(ii) A shallow-dose equivalent of 50 rem (0.5 Sv) to the skin of the whole body or to the skin of any extremity."

3. POINTS A RADIATION SAFETY REVIEWER MUST NOT GET WRONG

- Lens limit is 15 rem (0.15 Sv), not the pre-2007 value of 150 rem (1.5 Sv). The 2007 amendment (72 FR 68059, Dec. 4, 2007) lowered it by a factor of ten. Any procedure, dosimetry alarm setpoint, or ALARA investigation level still keyed to 150 rem is superseded.
- The 50 rem figure appears twice in § 20.1201 with different meanings: § 20.1201(a)(1)(ii) is 50 rems as the sum of deep-dose equivalent plus committed dose equivalent to any individual organ/tissue other than the lens; § 20.1201(a)(2)(ii) is 50 rem shallow-dose equivalent to skin. Same number, different quantity — do not merge them into a single line item.
- The whole-body limit is a two-part test: compliance requires meeting the more limiting of (a)(1)(i) TEDE = 5 rem and (a)(1)(ii) organ sum = 50 rem. The 5 rem TEDE value is normally the governing one.
- The skin limit is a shallow-dose equivalent averaged over the contiguous 10 square centimeters of skin receiving the highest exposure (§ 20.1201(c)); it is not a whole-body-averaged dose.
- Lens, skin, and extremity dose equivalents are not summed into the TEDE; they are subject to separate limits (§ 20.1202 note). Summation of external and internal dose under § 20.1202 applies to the TEDE/organ limits only.
- Additional constraints that ride alongside the (a) limits: soluble uranium intake limited to 10 mg/week for chemical toxicity (§ 20.1201(e)); the current-year limit must be reduced by occupational dose received while employed by any other person (§ 20.1201(f)); planned special exposures are capped at the numerical limit in any year and 5× the annual limit over a lifetime (§ 20.1206(e)).
- Related populations, for completeness: minors receive 10% of the adult limits (§ 20.1207), i.e. TEDE 0.5 rem (0.005 Sv), lens 1.5 rem (0.015 Sv), skin 5 rem (0.05 Sv); the embryo/fetus limit is 0.5 rem (0.005 Sv) over the gestation period (§ 20.1208).

4. COMPLIANCE-CHECK FORM

For each monitored adult, demonstrate compliance for the year by confirming all three of:
(1) TEDE (or deep-dose equivalent substituted per § 20.1201(c)) + committed effective dose equivalent from intake ≤ 5 rem (0.05 Sv);
(2) Lens dose equivalent ≤ 15 rem (0.15 Sv);
(3) Shallow-dose equivalent (max 10 cm² averaged) ≤ 50 rem (0.5 Sv).
Any single exceedance is an overexposure requiring report under § 20.2201/§ 20.2202 and dose-limit reduction for planned special exposures under § 20.1201(b).

Sources: eCFR § 20.1201 (fetched 2026-11-15); GovInfo CFR-2024-title10-vol1 XML and PDF of § 20.1201.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER — 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1) (Subpart M, Fall Protection; construction)

Governing text (verbatim):

  "(b) Guardrails, safety nets, and personal fall arrest systems. (1) Unprotected sides and edges. Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface) with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems."

1. TRIGGER HEIGHT

   6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level.

   - Measured from the walking/working surface on which the employee stands down to the lower level. "Lower level" per § 1926.500(b) means a surface or plane onto which an employee can fall — ground, floor, platform, ramp, roof, excavation bottom, water, machinery, etc.
   - The duty attaches AT 6 feet, not above it: 6 ft 0 in is covered. Anything strictly under 6 ft is outside (b)(1) (other Subpart M paragraphs may still apply — see § 4 below).
   - Applies to horizontal and vertical walking/working surfaces alike (the parenthetical in the text is deliberate: this covers wall/vertical surfaces as well as floors and roofs).
   - Applies whether the edge is a perimeter edge, an interior opening edge, or a floor/roof edge — the operative fact is that the side or edge is unprotected (i.e., not already guarded by a compliant system).
   - (b)(1) contains NO infeasibility exception and NO fall protection plan alternative. The "infeasible or creates a greater hazard → develop and implement a fall protection plan per § 1926.502(k)" exception, and its accompanying presumption note, appear in (b)(2)(i) (leading edges) only. Do not carry that exception into the unprotected-sides-and-edges determination.

2. ACCEPTABLE SYSTEMS — three, and only three, under (b)(1)

   (a) GUARDRAIL SYSTEMS — must meet § 1926.502(b). Key criteria:
       - Top edge height of top rail (or equivalent member) 42 inches ± 3 inches (1.1 m ± 8 cm) above the walking/working surface. (When conditions warrant, but only with the competent person's determination, top rail 45 inches ± 3 inches is permitted for certain circumstances per § 1926.502(b)(1).)
       - Midrail, screens, mesh, intermediate vertical members, or equivalent intermediate member between top rail and walking/working surface.
       - Must withstand, without failure, a force of at least 200 lb applied in any outward or downward direction at any point along the top edge (§ 1926.502(b)(3)).
       - No structural steel/other components that could puncture, lacerate, or snag; smooth-surfaced where employees may contact.
   (b) SAFETY NET SYSTEMS — must meet § 1926.502(c). Key criteria:
       - Installed as close as practicable under the walking/working surface, but in no case more than 30 feet (9.1 m) below that level (§ 1926.502(c)(1)).
       - Must be drop-tested (or certified/verified per § 1926.502(c)(2)–(4)) before use, and inspected at least weekly and after any impact.
       - Mesh openings, border rope, and connections per § 1926.502(c)(5)–(9); adequate clearance beneath to prevent contact with the surface or structures below.
   (c) PERSONAL FALL ARREST SYSTEMS — must meet § 1926.502(d). Key criteria:
       - Full-body harness, force distributed over at least the thighs, pelvis, waist, chest, and shoulders.
       - Limit maximum arresting force on an employee to 1,800 lb when used with a body harness (§ 1926.502(d)(15)).
       - Anchorage designed, installed, and used under supervision of a qualified person, capable of supporting at least 5,000 lb per employee attached, OR designed/installed as part of a complete system with a safety factor of at least two and certified by a qualified person (§ 1926.502(d)(15)).
       - Rigged so the employee can neither free-fall more than 6 feet (1.8 m) nor contact any lower level (§ 1926.502(d)(16)(ii)).
       - Bring the employee to a complete stop and limit maximum deceleration distance to 3.5 feet (1.1 m) (§ 1926.502(d)(16)(iii)).
       - Prompt rescue of any employee after a fall (§ 1926.502(d)(20)).

   Note: the § 1926.501(b) list is not a menu of equivalents. Where (b)(1) governs, one of these three must be used; covers, barricades, warning lines, designated areas, and fall protection plans are NOT (b)(1) substitutes (they are authorized only in other paragraphs — e.g., covers under (b)(4)/(b)(7)/(b)(11), controlled access zones under (b)(9), fall protection plans under (b)(2)(i)).

3. FIELD PROCEDURE (how to apply the answer on site)

   Step 1 — Identify the walking/working surface and each unprotected side or edge.
   Step 2 — Measure vertically from that surface to the lowest level the employee could fall to. Use the lowest credible fall surface, not the nearest.
   Step 3 — If the measured height is 6 ft (1.8 m) or more → protection is mandatory. Select at least one of: guardrail system, safety net system, personal fall arrest system.
   Step 4 — Verify the selected system against § 1926.502 (see § 2 criteria above) before exposing any employee; record the verification.
   Step 5 — If the height is under 6 ft, document that (b)(1) is not triggered, then screen against the other paragraphs in § 4 below before concluding no protection is required.
   Step 6 — Reassess whenever the working surface height, the lower level, or the edge protection condition changes.

4. CROSS-REFERENCES THAT DO NOT CHANGE THE (b)(1) ANSWER (listed to prevent misapplication)

   - § 1926.501(b)(2) Leading edges — also 6 ft (1.8 m); this is where the infeasibility/fall-protection-plan exception lives.
   - § 1926.501(b)(7)(ii) Excavations/wells/pits/shafts — 6 ft (1.8 m); guardrails, fences, barricades, or covers.
   - § 1926.501(b)(8) Dangerous equipment — protection required below 6 ft (equipment guards/guardrails) and at 6 ft or more (guardrails, PFAS, or nets).
   - § 1926.501(b)(9) Overhand bricklaying — 6 ft (1.8 m); adds controlled access zone as an option; 10-inch reach rule in (b)(9)(ii).
   - § 1926.501(b)(13) Residential construction — 6 ft (1.8 m) for employees engaged in residential construction activities.
   - § 1926.501(b)(14) Wall openings — 6 ft (1.8 m) outside bottom edge with inside bottom edge < 39 inches.
   - § 1926.501(b)(15) Walking/working surfaces not otherwise addressed — 6 ft (1.8 m).
   - § 1926.500(a)(2) — scope exclusions (e.g., certain scaffolds, ladders, and other specified situations covered by other Subpart M-referenced rules).
   - Other thresholds that are NOT the (b)(1) trigger and must not be substituted for it: general industry § 1910.28/1910.29 uses 4 ft; scaffolds § 1926.451(g)(1) uses 10 ft; steel erection § 1926.760 uses 15 ft (30 ft for connectors). Each governs its own scope only.
   - State plans: a State Plan may impose a stricter (lower) trigger height or additional systems; the federal 6 ft / three-system answer is the floor, not a ceiling, where an approved State Plan applies.

5. ONE-LINE ANSWER

   Six feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level, and protection must be by guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems — each installed and maintained per § 1926.502.

verdict.summary:
SCOPE AND ASSUMPTIONS

This answers the position for an adult worker in Great Britain under the Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833), as amended and currently in force. SI 1998/1833 extends to England and Wales and Scotland. Northern Ireland has an equivalent provision in the Working Time Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1998 (SR 1998/386), and the substance of the answer is the same there. The answer is a statement of the legal position, not advice on a particular contract or working pattern.

1. THE LIMIT UNDER REGULATION 4(1)

Regulation 4(1) of SI 1998/1833 provides (in its current amended form):

“Unless his employer has first obtained the worker’s agreement in writing to perform such work, a worker’s working time, including overtime, in any reference period which is applicable in his case shall not exceed an average of 48 hours for each seven days.”

Therefore the limit is an average of 48 hours per week — more precisely, 48 hours for each seven days — measured over the applicable reference period. It is not a hard cap of 48 hours in every individual week. Overtime is included to the extent that it is “working time”: time during which the worker is working, at the employer’s disposal and carrying out the employer’s activity or duties. Rest breaks, periods of leave and ordinary commuting are not working time.

Reference period. The default reference period is 17 weeks (regulation 4(3)(b)). Where a relevant agreement provides for the application of regulation 4 in relation to successive periods of 17 weeks, each such period is the reference period (regulation 4(3)(a)). Where the worker has worked for the employer for less than 17 weeks, the reference period is the period since the worker started work (regulation 4(4)). For a worker excluded from certain provisions by regulation 21, the references to 17 weeks are replaced by 26 weeks (regulation 4(5)). A relevant agreement under regulation 23(b) may also vary the reference period; that changes the averaging window, not the 48-hour average itself.

Calculation. Regulation 4(6) requires the average working time for each seven days during a reference period to be determined by the formula (A + B) / C, where A is the aggregate number of hours of working time during the reference period; B is the aggregate number of hours of working time during the period immediately after the reference period, ending when the number of days on which the worker has worked equals the number of excluded days in the reference period; and C is the number of weeks in the reference period. “Excluded days” under regulation 4(7) include days of annual leave under regulation 13 (and 13A or 15B), sick leave, maternity, paternity, adoption or parental leave, and days in respect of which the regulation 4(1) limit did not apply because the employer had obtained the worker’s written agreement.

Employer duty. Regulation 4(2) requires the employer to take all reasonable steps, in keeping with the need to protect workers’ health and safety, to ensure that the regulation 4(1) limit is complied with for each worker to whom it applies. The employer must also keep up-to-date records of workers who carry out work to which the limit does not apply because the employer has obtained the worker’s written agreement.

2. HOW A WORKER MAY BE TAKEN OUTSIDE THE LIMIT

The general route is the individual written opt-out. Regulation 4(1) disapplies the limit where the employer has first obtained the worker’s agreement in writing to perform such work. Regulation 5 then provides that the regulation 4(1) limit does not apply to a worker who has agreed with the employer in writing that it should not apply in the worker’s case. The agreement:

- must be in writing;
- may relate to a specified period or apply indefinitely;
- is terminable by the worker giving not less than seven days’ notice in writing, unless the agreement provides for a different period of notice; and
- where it provides for termination after a period of notice, that notice period must not exceed three months.

The agreement must be obtained before the worker performs the work that would exceed the limit. It may be a separate document or a written term in the contract, but it must evidence the worker’s agreement that the regulation 4(1) limit is not to apply. A unilateral employer statement, an oral agreement, implied consent, or a collective agreement alone does not take an individual worker outside regulation 4(1). The employer must keep up-to-date records identifying each worker who has agreed that the limit should not apply and setting out the terms on which the worker agreed.

Practical sequence:

1. Confirm the worker is an adult worker to whom regulation 4(1) applies and that no other stricter limit applies.
2. Before the worker performs work that would exceed the 48-hour average, obtain the worker’s written agreement that the regulation 4(1) limit should not apply.
3. Record the date, the scope of the agreement, whether it is for a specified period or indefinite, and any notice terms.
4. Give the worker a copy and explain the right to terminate the agreement on notice.
5. Keep the records up to date, including on withdrawal.
6. Continue to monitor hours: the opt-out disapplies only regulation 4(1). It does not remove the separate limits on night work, the rest and break provisions, the young-worker limits, or the employer’s general health and safety duties.

3. WHAT IS NOT A ROUTE OUT

The worker cannot be taken outside regulation 4(1) by the employer simply deciding not to apply it, by an oral arrangement, by a collective agreement alone, by a workforce agreement alone, or by recording long hours after the event. A relevant agreement under regulation 23(b) may vary the reference period, but it does not by itself disapply the 48-hour average. The route that disapplies regulation 4(1) for an individual adult worker is the worker’s own written agreement under regulation 5.

4. WORKER CATEGORIES AND TERRITORIAL NOTE

The 48-hour answer is the regulation 4(1) answer for an adult worker. Young workers are subject to the separate, stricter regime in regulation 5A: a young worker’s working time must not exceed eight hours a day or 40 hours a week, and there is no equivalent regulation 5 opt-out from that limit. Night workers are also subject to the separate average limit in regulation 6 (an average of eight hours for each 24 hours). In Northern Ireland, SR 1998/386 contains the equivalent 48-hour limit and written opt-out mechanism.

SHORT ANSWER

Ask 1 — Limit: 48 hours per week, being an average of 48 hours for each seven days over the applicable reference period, including overtime.

Ask 2 — How taken outside it: by the employer first obtaining the worker’s individual written agreement (the regulation 5 opt-out) that the regulation 4(1) limit should not apply in the worker’s case.
